title: Pierre Curie
author: Marie Curie
blurb: Marie Curie's own account of her husband: the crystals, the leaking shed, the tonnes of ore, the glowing tubes at night, and the rainy afternoon on the rue Dauphine.

p: Pierre Curie was born in Paris on 15 May 1859, into a family where knowledge was respected.
His father, Eugène Curie, was a doctor, and he himself would have liked to become a man of science.
He had never had the means to do research, but he passed on to his two sons his love of nature and of truth.
His mind was slow, or rather deep: he could not move quickly from one subject to another, as ordinary lessons demand.
When an idea interested him, he had to follow it to the very end, without being disturbed.
His parents understood that a child like him would be unhappy at school, and they taught him themselves, at home.
He spent long hours in the countryside around Paris, observing plants and animals.
Later, he often told me that those years of freedom had been the most precious of his life, because they had taught him to look.
At fourteen, he began to study mathematics with an excellent teacher, and his progress was rapid.
At sixteen, he passed his baccalauréat, and at eighteen, he already had his degree in physical sciences.
Very young, Pierre became a laboratory assistant at the Sorbonne: he helped the professors to prepare their experiments.
He worked with his older brother, Jacques, whom he loved deeply, and the two young men made a remarkable discovery together.
They showed that certain crystals, such as quartz, produce electricity when they are squeezed.
This phenomenon is called piezoelectricity, and it is used today in many devices.
Thanks to this discovery, the two brothers built a very sensitive instrument, capable of measuring tiny amounts of electricity.
Nobody could have guessed then that this device, fifteen years later, would allow us to discover radium.
In 1882, Pierre was appointed head of practical work at the School of Industrial Physics and Chemistry of the City of Paris.
He stayed there for twenty-two years. His salary was modest, and he did not even have a laboratory of his own.
Yet it was there that he carried out his great work on the symmetry of crystals and on magnetism.
He discovered, for example, that a magnet loses its magnetism when it is heated beyond a certain temperature.
Physicists still call this temperature the 'Curie point'.
I arrived in Paris from Warsaw in 1891, to study at the Sorbonne.
I lived alone in a little room under the roof, where it was so cold in winter that the water froze in my washbasin.
But I was happy: at last, I could learn.
In the spring of 1894, I needed a laboratory to study the magnetic properties of steel.
A Polish friend, the physicist Kowalski, invited me to his home, telling me that a young scientist might be able to help me.
When I came in, Pierre Curie was standing by the window.
He seemed very young to me, although he was then thirty-five. He had clear eyes, a serious and gentle expression, and a simplicity that struck me immediately.
We talked about science, then about social questions, and I had the feeling that we thought the same way about almost everything.
Pierre wanted us to spend our lives together, but I hesitated.
I had always thought that I would go back to Poland to serve my country, and I did not want to abandon it.
He then wrote me letters that I kept all my life.
In one of them, he told me it would be beautiful to share our dreams, and to make of life a dream, and of a dream a reality.
We were married on 26 July 1895, in Sceaux, very simply: we had no white dress, no wedding rings and no wedding feast.
With the money a relative had given us, we bought two bicycles, and we set off on the roads of France.
In 1896, the physicist Henri Becquerel had discovered that uranium gives off invisible rays, with no outside cause.
These rays passed through black paper and made the air conduct electricity.
Nobody understood where this energy came from. I decided to make it the subject of my thesis.
To measure these rays, I used the electrometer that Pierre and his brother had invented.
I examined a great many minerals, and I soon found that thorium, too, gave off rays.
But one result surprised me greatly: certain ores, such as pitchblende, were much more active than the uranium they contained.
So they had to contain another substance, unknown and much more radioactive.
Pierre understood the importance of this hypothesis, and he gave up his own research to work with me.
In July 1898, we announced the discovery of a new element, which we called 'polonium', in honour of my country.
In December of the same year, we announced a second one: 'radium'.
We worked in an old abandoned shed, at the far end of the courtyard of the School of Physics.
Its glass roof let the rain in, and in winter the temperature did not rise above six degrees.
A German chemist who visited us said later that it could have been mistaken for a stable.
And yet it was in that shed that we spent the most beautiful years of our lives.
For chemists to believe in radium's existence, we had to isolate it: we had to show it, weigh it, measure its atomic weight.
But there were only tiny traces of it in the ore.
Thanks to the Austrian government, we received several tonnes of pitchblende residues, which came from the mines of Joachimsthal, in Bohemia.
I processed up to twenty kilos of material at a time.
I spent whole days stirring a boiling mass with an iron bar almost as tall as me, and in the evening I was worn out with fatigue.
Pierre, for his part, studied the properties of the rays. We talked of nothing but our work, pacing up and down in the shed.
Our daughter Irène had been born in 1897, and we also had to look after her and the house.
Sometimes, in the evening, after putting her to bed, we went back to the laboratory.
In the darkness, our tubes and flasks glowed softly on the shelves, like little fairy lights.
That sight always moved us, and we would stay a long time contemplating it in silence.
In 1902, after almost four years of work, I finally obtained a decigram of pure radium chloride, and I was able to measure its atomic weight.
Radium existed. From then on, nobody could doubt it any more.
In 1903, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to us, together with Henri Becquerel.
Overnight we became famous, and our peaceful life was turned upside down.
Journalists came right into the laboratory; strangers wrote to us from all over the world; we were invited everywhere.
Pierre suffered greatly from it. He said that fame stole from him the time he needed to think.
He did not like honours. When they wanted to give him the Legion of Honour, he replied that he had no need to be decorated, but that he had the greatest need of a laboratory.
We also refused to take out a patent on our method of preparing radium.
We could have become rich, but that seemed to us contrary to the spirit of science: our discoveries had to belong to everyone.
We did not yet know how dangerous radium was.
Pierre had deliberately left a tube of radium on his arm for several hours, to study its effects: the burn had taken weeks to heal.
Our hands were damaged, and we were often exhausted, without understanding why.
In 1904, Pierre was finally appointed professor at the Sorbonne, and our second daughter, Ève, was born in December of the same year.
19 April 1906 was a grey, rainy Thursday.
Pierre had had lunch with colleagues, then he had gone out, under his umbrella, to go to his publisher's.
While crossing the rue Dauphine, he slipped on the wet cobblestones, right in front of a heavy cart drawn by two horses.
He fell, and a wheel crushed his head. He died instantly.
I cannot describe what I felt that day.
In one instant I had lost my husband, my companion in work, and the best friend I have ever had.
For months, I went on living and working like an automaton, speaking to him in my heart as if he were still there.
The Sorbonne offered me his course. I accepted, because it was the only way to continue his work.
On 5 November 1906, I entered the crowded lecture hall.
It was the first time a woman had taught at the Sorbonne, and many people had come out of curiosity.
I took up the course exactly at the sentence where Pierre had left it.
Those who knew Pierre remember above all his kindness and his modesty.
He never sought positions or money. He did not know how to put himself forward, and he did not understand why anyone would.
He treated a minister and a laboratory boy in the same way.
For him, science was not a profession, but a way of living.
He believed that it would one day make people better and happier, provided they used it wisely.
He often said that humanity needs practical people, but that it also needs dreamers, for whom disinterested research is so captivating that they have no time to think of their own interest.
After his death, I devoted my strength to fulfilling the dream he had not lived to see: a real laboratory, worthy of the science he loved.
The Radium Institute was built in Paris, in a street that today bears his name: the rue Pierre-et-Marie-Curie.
I often think that it is there, more than in books, that he lives on: in every young researcher who enters the laboratory wanting to understand.
